prefill.d: First phase of inference: all prompt tokens go through the model together (in chunks of up to max_num_batched_tokens), and each layer writes their K and V into the KV cache. With large \(M\), it is mostly compute-bound; it ends at the first token (TTFT).

gemm.d: Multiplication \(Y = XW\) with several rows in \(X\) (\(M > 1\)). Each weight read from memory is reused by \(M\) rows, which raises the arithmetic intensity. It is the typical operation of prefill.

gemv.d: Multiplication of a weight matrix by a single activation vector (\(M = 1\)). Each weight read takes part in just one multiplication: intensity ≈ \(2/b_w\) FLOP/B. It is the operation of single-sequence decode and the reason decode is bandwidth-bound.

flops.d: Floating-point operations. A multiply-accumulate counts as 2 FLOPs, which is why \(Y = XW\) costs \(2MKN\). “FLOPS” (with a capital S, per second) measures a GPU's speed; the GB10 sits around ~125 dense BF16 TFLOPS (the recipes' estimate).

intensidade-aritmetica.d: FLOPs executed per byte brought from main memory (\(I = F/Q\)). For a projection where weights dominate the bytes, \(I \approx 2M/b_w\); when activations weigh in (large M, or 4-bit weights with BF16 activations), use the full formula \(2MKN / (b_w KN + b_a M(K+N))\). Compared with the ridge (\(P_{\text{peak}}/\beta\), ~458 FLOP/B on the GB10 in BF16), it tells whether the kernel is memory-bound or compute-bound.

roofline.d: Performance model (Williams, Waterman and Patterson, 2009): attainable performance is \(\min(P_{\text{peak}}, I\cdot\beta)\), where \(P_{\text{peak}}\) is the compute peak and \(\beta\) the bandwidth. On a log-log scale, it is a ramp (bandwidth limit) that meets a flat ceiling (compute peak) at the ridge point.

ridge-point.d: Arithmetic intensity \(I^* = P_{\text{peak}}/\beta\) at which the bandwidth limit and the compute limit tie on the roofline. On the GB10: ~125 TFLOPS ÷ 273 GB/s ≈ 458 FLOP/B in BF16. To the left, the kernel waits for data; to the right, the data waits for the kernel.

memory-bound.d: Regime in which the kernel's time is dominated by moving bytes (\(Q/\beta > F/P\)): the tensor cores sit idle waiting for data. It is decode with small \(M\), and also the experts of an MoE when each one receives few rows.

compute-bound.d: Regime in which the kernel's time is dominated by arithmetic operations (\(F/P > Q/\beta\)), to the right of the roofline's ridge. It is dense prefill with large \(M\).

banda-de-memoria.d: Bytes per second that memory delivers to the GPU. On the GB10, the unified LPDDR5X has ~273 GB/s theoretical and 230–250 GB/s effective as measured by the recipes, and it is what sets the decode ceiling: tok/s ≈ tokens per step × bandwidth ÷ bytes read per step.

streaming-de-pesos.d: Continuous reading of the active weights from memory at every decode step. When it dominates the step (DeepSeek c=1: “~80% weight streaming”), fewer bytes per weight (quantization), fewer active weights (MoE) and more tokens per read (speculation, batching) are the levers.

mascara-causal.d: The attention rule of a decoder: token \(t\) only sees tokens \(j \le t\). Because of it, the state of a past token never changes with the future, which is why its K and V can be computed once and stored in the KV cache.

bytes-por-token.d: Memory each context token takes up in the KV cache: \(L_{kv} \times n_{kv} \times (d_k + d_v) \times b\), summed over all layers that store KV. Qwen 26,624 B (BF16) / 13,312 B (FP8); GLM 7,579 B per rank; DeepSeek ≈3,850 B. It determines how many tokens fit in the pool.

estado-fixo.d: Memory a sequence takes up regardless of its length: the recurrent state of the linear attention layers (GDN in Qwen, KDA in GLM, ~76 MiB per request per rank) and the sliding windows (≈3.44 MB in DeepSeek). It is added to \(c \times\) bytes per token.

pool-de-kv.d: Memory left, after weights, activations and buffers, for the KV cache of all conversations together. Divided by the bytes per token, it gives the total number of live tokens that fit; max_model_len and max_num_seqs are ceilings, not reservations, on this pool.

ttft.d: Time between sending the request and the first token of the response: queue + prefill + first sampling. With an idle server and a cold cache, it measures prefill (prefill tok/s = prompt tokens ÷ TTFT). With reasoning on, it also includes the thinking.

tpot.d: Average time per output token, excluding the first: \((t_N - t_1)/(N-1)\). It is the inverse of decode's per-stream tok/s and describes the reading speed the user perceives.

itl.d: Interval between two consecutive events in a request's stream. Without speculation, it matches the TPOT; with speculation, each event carries several tokens and the ITL ends up measuring the time of one step.

prefill-tok-s.d: Prompt tokens ÷ TTFT. It is not constant: it rises while the fixed per-request costs get diluted and then drops when attention and the indexer grow with the context (DeepSeek 0731: 447 tok/s with 256 tokens, 2,563 with 2,048, 1,713 with 8,192, 1,428 with 32,768, 1,665 with 131,072). Only valid with an idle server and a cold prefix cache.

tok-s-por-stream.d: Decode speed as seen by one user (1/TPOT). It drops as concurrency rises, because the step gets longer: in Qwen, from 54.4 tok/s with 1 stream to 26.7 with 8.

tok-s-agregado.d: Sum of the tokens of all concurrent requests ÷ burst duration: the machine's capacity. It rises with concurrency while the marginal cost per sequence is small (Qwen: 54.4 → 207.0 tok/s from 1 to 8 streams).

amortizacao-de-pesos.d: Processing \(B\) sequences in the same decode step so that a single read of the weights serves all of them. With \(t(B) \approx T_0 + B\,T_1\), the aggregate grows until it approaches \(\tau/T_1\). In an MoE it pays off less, because more tokens light up more distinct experts.
